solution:
Five, as listed in the map's index: agriculture, animal husbandry, fishing, mining and lumbering.

The chapter adds hunting and gathering to the list of primary economic activities, but those two are not shown on this map.

Antarctica carries no symbol of any kind, and the far northern edges of the continents carry almost none.

The reason is the climate. The chapter states that all these activities are dependent on nature, and Antarctica is permanently ice-covered, so there is no soil for agriculture, no grass for animal husbandry and no forest for lumbering. Its minerals are not worked either, because as the chapter notes actual mining depends on the geology of the region, climate, capital investment, technology and skilled labour, and the climate there defeats all of them.

Mainly in the higher middle and high latitudes, roughly north of 45 to 50 degrees N, in a broad belt running across the far north of North America, Europe and Asia.

That is where the coniferous forests lie, and the chapter explains why lumbering concentrates there: in the coniferous forests only one species of trees is found in an area and these trees grow tall, which is why in the world the lumbering activity is mostly practised in the coniferous regions.

A few scattered symbols also appear in the tropics, but not as a continuous belt.

Because the conditions that produce fish in commercial quantity occur only in certain places, and the map's blue bands mark exactly those.

The chapter names the two decisive physical conditions. The first is a wide expanse of continental shelf with shallow water, which is why the bands hug the coasts and the banks rather than the open ocean. The second is the confluence of warm and cold currents and the growth of abundant plankton that follows, as a result of which fishing grounds or banks develop; its example is the meeting of the warm Kuroshio current with the cold Oyashio current, which favours the coastal area near Japan.

Human conditions narrow it further: traditional fishing skills, dependence on fish as a staple food, absence of an alternative occupation, a broken coastline giving port facilities, and a cold climate that allows fish to be preserved.

Agriculture covers most of Europe, and mining stars are scattered across it. Fishing bands lie along its north-western coasts, and lumbering symbols run across its far north.

So all five activities appear, but agriculture is the one that covers the largest area.

Offshore mineral oil and natural gas production.

The chapter states that man has even started exploiting the mineral oil and natural gas reserves from the sea and ocean beds too, so a mining symbol in the sea marks that rather than the mining of solid minerals.
Antarctica. Mining stars appear on every other continent, and also offshore in the seas, but Antarctica carries no symbol of any kind.

The Pacific Ocean, and within it the north-west Pacific in particular, where the blue band runs from the Okhotsk Sea down along the coasts of Japan and China.

The chapter gives the reason for that concentration twice over: the north-west Pacific has a wide continental shelf in water below 200 metres deep near the Okhotsk Sea, and the warm Kuroshio current meets the cold Oyashio current there, producing the plankton on which the fishing grounds depend.

South of the Tropic of Capricorn the map shows agriculture along the coastal margins of Australia, southern Africa and southern South America; animal husbandry over the interior of Australia and of southern South America; fishing bands off the west coast of South America, off southern Africa and around south-east Australia; and mining stars in all three.

Lumbering symbols are few there, because the great coniferous belt lies in the northern hemisphere and there is little land in these latitudes to carry one.

Lumbering. The islands of South East Asia carry lumbering symbols, along with agriculture.

The chapter notes that these are equatorial evergreen forests, and lists South East Asia among the regions where such lumbering is carried on, though it also explains why it stays small in scale there: the forests are dense and difficult to reach, they carry many species in a small area, the climate is inhospitable, and hardwood is less in demand than softwood.

Australia has the least agriculture of the four. The green agriculture shading is confined to its coastal margins, and the whole of its interior is under animal husbandry instead.

The interior of Australia is arid, and the chapter's account of animal husbandry explains why the two divide that way: animal husbandry develops in the dry interiors of continents where grasslands rather than crops are possible.

[Note: the question says 'all the four continents' but does not say which four, so the comparison above is between the continents the map shades most heavily for agriculture: North America, Europe, Asia and Australia.]

On the map agriculture is spread through the middle latitudes and the tropics but stops before the far north, and it is thickest where the climate is neither extreme nor arid: eastern North America, Europe, south and east Asia, eastern South America and the coastal margins of Australia.

Climate sets the outer limits. Beyond about 60 degrees N the growing season is too short and the ground frozen for too much of the year, so the belt that carries lumbering carries almost no crops. Within the tropics agriculture is heavy in the monsoon lands of south and east Asia, where rain is reliable, but thin over the Sahara and the interior of Australia, where it is not. So the northern limit is set by temperature and the gaps inside the tropics are set by rainfall.

That is why the same latitude can carry very different results. Europe and Asia at 50 degrees N are under crops while central Asia at the same latitude is under animal husbandry, because latitude decides the heat a place receives but not the water it receives.

The chapter puts the same point in its list of influences: the major physical factors that influence agriculture are climate, topography, soils and biotic factors, and climate stands first among them.

| Primary economic activity | Natural resources required | Natural factors affecting it | Man-made factors affecting it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Agriculture | Land, soil, water, air | Slope of land, quality of soil, favourable climate, rainfall | Fertilizers, insecticides, farm machines |
| Animal husbandry | Grassland, fodder, water | Climate, presence of grasslands, quality of fodder | Advanced technology, market, availability of large estates |
| Fishing | Fish, sea water, continental shelf | Wide continental shelf with shallow water, confluence of warm and cold currents, growth of plankton, cold climate, broken coastline | Traditional fishing skills, technology, port facilities, refrigeration, wood for ship building |
| Mining | Minerals in the earth's crust | Geology of the region, climate | Capital investment, technology, skilled labour, transportation facilities, mechanisation |
| Lumbering | Forest, trees | Type of forest, density of forest, hardness of the wood, accessibility, climate | Machinery, transportation, demand in the market |
| Gathering | Forest products such as fruits, roots, tubers, leaves, flowers, medicinal plants, gum, lac, honey, wax, rubber | Type of forest, density of the forest, climate, insects and reptiles | Market demand, manual labour |

Every row draws on factors the chapter itself names for that activity, which is why mining's natural column is thin: the chapter says mining depends solely on the presence of minerals and is not related to latitude directly.

In the monsoon region the map shows lumbering symbols in the countries of south and south-east Asia, above all India and the countries of the Indo-Chinese peninsula and the Indonesian islands.

The chapter notes that tropical deciduous or monsoon forests are not dense and have many bushes at the base, and that because they lie near agricultural land and densely populated regions they have been deforested for agricultural purposes on a large scale.
In the eastern and south-eastern parts of Australia, where the lumbering symbols lie along the wetter coastal margin. The dry interior carries animal husbandry instead.

Because northern Africa is desert. The Sahara covers almost the whole of it, and where there is no forest there can be no lumbering.

The chapter's framing applies directly: lumbering is one of the activities going on in the forest, and the earth is divided into natural regions according to the nature of the vegetation. A region with no tree cover falls outside every one of the four forest types in Table 4.2.

Latitude decides the type of forest, and the type of forest decides whether lumbering is worth doing, so the activity ends up concentrated in a particular latitude band.

In the high latitudes, roughly beyond 45 to 50 degrees N, lie the coniferous forests. The chapter says that in these forests only one species of trees is found in an area and the trees grow tall, which is why lumbering is mostly practised in the coniferous regions of the world. The map bears this out: the lumbering belt runs across the far north of North America, Europe and Asia.

In the equatorial latitudes the forests are dense and evergreen with many species in a small area, the wood is hard, access is difficult and the climate inhospitable, so commercial lumbering cannot be done there.

In the tropical deciduous or monsoon belt between them the forests are not dense, but they lie near agricultural land and dense population and have largely been cleared for farming.

So lumbering is not spread evenly through the latitudes: it is a high-latitude activity by nature, with only scattered occurrences elsewhere.

Because everything about an equatorial forest works against commercial felling.

The trees are hardwood and the forest is evergreen, and the chapter states plainly that commercial lumbering cannot be done in these forests for that reason.

Table 4.2 gives the rest. The forests are dense, which increases inaccessibility and creates transportation problems. Many species grow in a small area, so a stand of one useful timber cannot be worked economically. Insects and reptiles cause problems for the workers, and the climate is inhospitable. Methods remain traditional. And hardwood is comparatively less in demand than softwood, so even the timber that is cut finds a smaller market.

| Type of forest | Regions | Characteristics of forests | Characteristics of lumbering activity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Equatorial Evergreen forests | Amazon river basin in South America, Congo river basin of Africa, West coast of Africa, South East Asia, Papua New Guinea | Dense forests; many species in a small area; hard wood trees; accessibility is difficult; inhospitable climate | Dense forests increase inaccessibility and transportation issues; traditional methods; insects and reptiles cause problems; hard wood less in demand than softwood; many species in one region makes it unprofitable |
| Tropical Deciduous forest (Monsoon) | South and South East Asia, including India | Not dense; many bushes grow at the base; trees shed their leaves in the dry season; lie close to agricultural land and densely populated regions | Carried on, but on a limited scale; much of the forest has been deforested for agricultural purposes rather than worked for timber; access is easier than in the equatorial forests because the forest is open |
| Temperate deciduous forest | Eastern North America, Western and Central Europe, East Asia | Less dense than equatorial forest; hardwood trees; fewer species in an area | Commercial lumbering is possible, and access is easier because the regions are developed and well served by transport |
| Temperate Coniferous forest | The far north of North America, Europe and Asia, in a broad belt | Only one species of trees is found in an area; the trees grow tall; softwood | The lumbering activity is mostly practised here; a single species over a large area makes working the forest economic, and softwood is in greater demand |

[Note: the chapter gives the equatorial row in full and states the key facts for the monsoon and coniferous forests, but it does not describe the temperate deciduous forest or name regions for any row except the equatorial one. Those cells follow the pattern the chapter sets out rather than statements it makes.]
Along the north-eastern coast of North America, in the north-west Atlantic. The map names the Grand Bank there, together with the Sable Bank and the Georges Bank.
Along the western coast of South America, where the map's blue fishing band runs down the Pacific side of the continent.
In the south-eastern part of Australia, where the blue fishing band follows the coast. The northern and western coasts carry much less.

Because the physical conditions the chapter names for a fishing ground are met on the western coast and not on the eastern one.

The western coast has a wider continental shelf with shallow water, and it lies where cold water meets warm. The chapter states that the confluence of warm and cold currents and the growth of abundant plankton that follows is what causes fishing grounds or banks to develop, and it is that plankton which supports the fish.

The cooler water on the western side also helps in a second way the chapter names: a cold climate facilitates the preservation of fish, whereas in warm tropical waters artificial refrigeration facilities have to be developed first.

[Note: the chapter gives the general conditions for a fishing ground but does not discuss the two coasts of Africa, so the application above is inferred from those conditions rather than stated.]

Because the southern coast of Greenland has the combination of conditions the chapter lists.

It lies in the north-west Atlantic where warm and cold currents meet, and the chapter states that such a confluence and the growth of abundant plankton that follows is what causes fishing grounds or banks to develop. The continental shelf there is wide and the water shallow, which is the first of the physical factors it names.

The climate helps rather than hinders. A cold climate in the temperate regions facilitates the preservation of fish, so the catch can be kept without artificial refrigeration.

The coastline is deeply broken by fjords, and the chapter notes that a broken coast line provides excellent port facilities. Finally, the absence of an alternative occupation makes fishing a major occupation, which is the chapter's third human factor and applies to a land with almost no cultivable ground.

[Note: the chapter does not discuss Greenland itself, so the reasons above apply its general conditions to that coast.]

Yes, a close one. On the map the tan animal-husbandry shading lies over the interiors of the continents, which is where the grasslands are: the interior of North America, central and western Asia, the interior of South America, the interior and east of Australia and the belt south of the Sahara.

The chapter states the link directly: the presence of grasslands in all the continents has led to the distribution of this occupation.

Africa, apart from a belt south of the Sahara, and Antarctica not at all. Of the inhabited continents, animal husbandry is least developed on a large commercial scale in Africa.

The chapter names the three where it has developed commercially: North America, South America and Australia. It explains the gap in Africa when it says that dense forests, an inhospitable climate and low-quality fodder in the equatorial region have discouraged the development of animal husbandry there, and it adds that the occupation is influenced by advanced technology, market and the availability of large estates, all of which are limited in much of Africa.

They coincide over wide areas of the middle latitudes: the central and eastern parts of North America, Europe, parts of southern and eastern Asia, south-eastern South America and the coastal margins of Australia. On the map the green and tan shadings meet and overlap along these margins.

The chapter draws the conclusion from the same map: looking at fig. 4.1 we realise that agriculture and animal husbandry are done together in many areas, and hence they are considered as allied activities.

Between 30 degrees N and 60 degrees N in the northern hemisphere, and between 30 degrees S and 55 degrees S in the southern hemisphere. The chapter states these limits directly, and adds that the occupation is more developed in the northern hemisphere.

In the equatorial zone, the belt on either side of the equator.

The chapter gives three reasons together: dense forests, an inhospitable climate and low-quality fodder in the equatorial region have discouraged the development of animal husbandry there. Dense forest leaves no open grazing land, the humid heat is hard on livestock, and the grass that does grow is poor feed.

This is why the chapter's latitude limits start at 30 degrees on each side of the equator rather than at the equator itself.

Because eastern Australia has the grassland the activity depends on, in a climate that suits it, at a distance from the desert interior.

The chapter names the three conditions under which animal husbandry becomes commercial: advanced technology, market and the availability of large estates. Eastern Australia has all three, and the chapter lists Australia with North and South America among the regions where the occupation has developed on a commercial basis.

It also lies within the 30 to 55 degrees S band that the chapter gives as the southern-hemisphere limit of the activity.

Because the arid interiors have the grass and not the rain.

The chapter states that the presence of grasslands in all the continents has led to the distribution of this occupation, and the temperate grasslands lie in exactly those interior positions: too dry for reliable cropping, but able to carry grass over great areas.

Land of that kind is also cheap and available in large blocks, which matters because the chapter names the availability of large estates as one of the three things that make animal husbandry commercial, along with advanced technology and market.

So the interior is not chosen in spite of its dryness but because of it: where crops cannot be grown, grazing is the productive use of the land.

Mining stars are scattered over most of North America, but they are thickest in the eastern part of the continent and along the western mountain belt, with a further concentration in the far north.

The chapter explains why the pattern is irregular rather than banded: the distribution of minerals is highly uneven in the world, and this activity depends solely on the presence of minerals.
Along the western, Pacific side of South America, where the mining stars follow the line of the Andes, with further stars in the east of the continent.

No. Mining is the one primary activity on the map that shows no latitudinal band at all: its stars are scattered across every continent except Antarctica, from the far north to the southern tips.

The chapter states the reason directly: the distribution of minerals is highly uneven in the world, and this activity depends solely on the presence of minerals and is not related to latitude directly.

That is what separates it from the others on the map. Lumbering follows the forest belts, animal husbandry lies between 30 and 60 degrees, agriculture thins towards the poles and fishing follows the shelves and current confluences, because all of those depend on climate or on living things that depend on climate. Minerals were placed by geology, not by climate.

The chapter does add that whether a known mineral is actually mined depends on further factors, among them the geology of the region, the value of the mineral, climate, capital investment, technology and skilled labour, so climate enters at the second stage but not the first.

Yes, though the relation runs from mining to development rather than the other way round.

The chapter traces the chain: due to mechanisation this occupation has developed on a large scale, many industries related to minerals locate near mining areas, improved transportation facilities are very important for the development of mining, and this in turn increases industries, which in turn leads to the economic development of the country.

The relation is not automatic, because whether minerals in the ground are worked at all depends on capital investment, technology and skilled labour, and those are themselves marks of a developed economy. So a country with minerals and no capital may mine little, while a developed country works even low-value deposits.

| Characteristics | Type of Agriculture |
|---|---|
| 1) Small land holding, maximum yield from small land, food crops dominant, manual labour, China, India, Japan, Korea, Sri Lanka, rice the major crop | D) Intensive Subsistence Agriculture |
| 2) Large farm, capital intensive, modern machinery from sowing to harvesting, monoculture, temperate grassland, Steppes, Praries, Downs, Pampas, Velds, wheat and maize | F) Extensive Commercial Agriculture |
| 3) Large farm, capital intensive, monoculture, local labour, crop managed for quality and processing, production for 10 to 15 years, tea, coffee, rubber, cocoa | E) Plantation Agriculture |
| 4) Forest land burnt, very small farm, production for only 2 to 3 years, land left fallow, soil erosion, forested tropical regions | A) Shifting Agriculture |
| 5) Modern, in fringe areas serving urban demand, maximum production from limited area, high capital, vegetables, fruits, milk, eggs, within an overnight truck journey | C) Market Gardening |
| 6) Fruits, flowers, medicinal and ornamental plants for commercial use, manual labour and mechanization, tropical, Mediterranean and temperate regions | B) Horticulture |

The two pairs that are easiest to confuse are worth separating. Rows 2 and 3 are both large, capital-intensive and monocultural, but row 2 is machine-worked temperate grain on grassland while row 3 is labour-worked tropical tree crops. Rows 5 and 6 both grow high-value produce, but row 5 is defined by its position near a city and row 6 by what it grows.

| Physical factors | Human (economic and social) factors |
|---|---|
| Climate | Labour |
| Topography | Market |
| Soils | Capital |
| Biotic factors | Transportation facilities |
| | Storage facilities |
| | Government policies |
| | Population |
| | Ownership of land |

The chapter gives both lists: the major physical factors that influence agriculture are climate, topography, soils and biotic factors, and the economic and social factors include labour, market, capital, transportation facilities, storage facilities, government policies, population and ownership of land.

It adds a group that sits between the two, being human means of overcoming a physical limit: greenhouses and polyhouses, high-yielding seeds, fertilizers and insecticides, all used for increasing production.

| A | B | C |
|---|---|---|
| 1) Intensive Subsistence agriculture | 3) Rice | 1) Small size of farm |
| 2) Pampas Grassland region | 5) Commercial animal husbandry | 5) South America |
| 3) Fishing | 1) Dogger Bank | 4) NE Atlantic Ocean |
| 4) Gathering | 4) Dense forest | 2) Unfavorable |
| 5) Mining | 2) Off shore oil and gas production | 3) Bombay High |

Each chain runs activity, then what it produces or where it happens, then the place or condition that goes with it.

Intensive subsistence agriculture grows rice on small holdings, which the chapter gives as its first two characteristics. The Pampas is temperate grassland, and the chapter lists the Pampas among the grasslands of extensive commercial agriculture, where cultivation and commercial animal husbandry are done together. The Dogger Bank is a fishing ground in the north-east Atlantic. Gathering depends on dense forest, and conditions there are unfavourable, which the chapter explains for the equatorial forests: the climate is humid and unhealthy and reptiles and insects disturb the work, so collection is not done on a large scale. Mining now reaches offshore oil and gas, which the chapter notes when it says man has started exploiting the mineral oil and natural gas reserves from the sea and ocean beds, and Bombay High is such a field.

Plantation agriculture is a large-scale, capital-intensive, commercial form of cultivation practised mainly in the tropics.

Its farms are large and capital intensive, and it is monocultural, one crop being grown over the whole estate. Local labour is employed. The crop is well managed for quality and for processing, so the produce usually leaves the estate part-processed.

Its yield per hectare is low but its total production is high, because of the area under it. Once a plantation is established it gives production for ten to fifteen years, so the investment is recovered over a long period.

The crops are tea, coffee, rubber and cocoa, with spice plantations in Kerala and cashewnut plantations in the Konkan region. The chapter names Malaysia, India, Sri Lanka, Brazil, Indonesia, the Caribbean Islands, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam among the countries where it is practised.

The chapter names two physical factors as decisive for fishing.

The first is a wide expanse of continental shelf with the presence of shallow water. Its example is the north-west Pacific, which is below 200 metres of depth near the Okhotsk Sea near China.

The second is the confluence of warm and cold currents and the subsequent growth of abundant plankton. As a result of this, fishing grounds or banks develop. Its example is the meeting of the warm Kuroshio current with the cold Oyashio current, which favours the coastal area near Japan for fishing.

Two more physical conditions appear in the chapter's wider list. A broken coast line provides excellent port facilities. And a cold climate in the temperate regions facilitates the preservation of fish, whereas in tropical countries artificial refrigeration facilities have to be developed instead.

The map shows the result: the fishing bands lie over the shelves and the banks and along the coasts where cold and warm water meet, not in the open ocean.

Commercial lumbering is the felling of timber for the market rather than for local use, and the chapter shows that it is possible only in certain forests.

It is concentrated in the coniferous forests. There only one species of trees is found in an area and the trees grow tall, which is why the chapter says lumbering is mostly practised in the coniferous regions of the world. A single species over a large area can be worked with machinery and sold as one product, and softwood is in greater demand than hardwood.

It cannot be done in the equatorial forests. Their trees are hardwood and the forests evergreen, and the chapter states for that reason that commercial lumbering cannot be done in these forests. Dense growth makes them inaccessible and creates transportation problems, many species grow in a small area, insects and reptiles cause problems, and the climate is inhospitable.

In the tropical deciduous or monsoon forests the forest is not dense, but because it lies near agricultural land and densely populated regions it has largely been cleared for agriculture rather than worked for timber.

The chapter closes with the cost: wood is used on a very large scale for various purposes, so the percentage of forest in the world is decreasing drastically, and hazards related to the environment are occurring as a result.

Hunting was a primitive activity by which man obtained food, and it is the oldest of the primary economic activities.

Its cost to the ecosystem has been heavy. The chapter states that a large number of animal species have become extinct or are on the verge of extinction because of large-scale hunting.

The response has been prohibition. Commercial hunting is banned all over the world, and many laws are being passed to conserve and protect animals.

What remains is subsistence hunting by a few communities. The chapter names the Bushmen of the Kalahari desert in South Africa, the Pygmies of the equatorial Selvas, the Boras, the Eskimos of the Tundra, and the Sentinels, Jarawahs and Onges in the Andaman islands as people who still hunt for a livelihood.

The loss matters beyond the species themselves, because removing animals from a forest breaks the food chain and the ecological balance that the chapter elsewhere lists among the things studied in the biosphere.

Because India has both the conditions for cultivation and the population that depends on it.

The physical factors favour it. The chapter names climate, topography, soils and biotic factors as the major physical influences on agriculture, and India has extensive plains, fertile soils and a monsoon climate with a reliable wet season.

The human factors reinforce it. The chapter states that the proportion of people engaged in agriculture is maximum in Africa and then in Asia, and that the share of population engaged in agriculture is higher in developing countries, while developed countries have less. India belongs to the second group.

The type of agriculture follows from that. The chapter's account of intensive subsistence agriculture describes India directly: small land holdings, maximum yield taken from a small area, food crops dominant, manual labour and the use of animals, with rice as the major crop, practised in China, India, Japan, Korea, Sri Lanka and the East Asian countries.

India also carries commercial forms alongside it, with the chapter naming spice plantations in Kerala and cashewnut plantations in the Konkan region.

Because the minerals are there, which is the one condition the chapter says mining cannot do without.

It states that the distribution of minerals is highly uneven in the world and that this activity depends solely on the presence of minerals, and the Chhota Nagpur plateau is one of the mineral-rich regions of India.

The secondary conditions are met as well. The chapter lists the geology of the region, the value of the minerals, climate, capital investment, technology and skilled labour as the factors on which actual mining depends, and adds that improved transportation facilities are very important for the development of mining.

The result is the chain the chapter describes: many industries related to minerals locate near mining areas, which increases industries, which in turn leads to the economic development of the region.

[Note: the chapter names the Chhota Nagpur plateau only in the exercise question itself. Its mineral wealth is treated as known; the reasoning above applies the chapter's general conditions for mining to it.]

Because Canada lies in the great coniferous belt, which is the forest type commercial lumbering depends on.

The chapter states that in the coniferous forests only one species of trees is found in an area and that these trees grow tall, and that this is why lumbering is mostly practised in the coniferous regions of the world. A single tall species over a large area can be felled by machine and sold as one product, and its softwood is in greater demand than hardwood.

The map shows the belt running across the far north of North America, and the northern part of Canada lies within it.

The comparison with the alternatives completes the reason. Equatorial forests cannot be worked commercially at all, because they are dense, many-speciesed, hardwood, inaccessible and inhospitable; monsoon forests have largely been cleared for agriculture. The coniferous forest is what is left.

Because everything about it is organised for sale rather than for the household.

The chapter's characteristics say so one by one. The farm is large in size and capital intensive, with more use of modern machinery, and machinery is used from sowing to harvesting. The farming is monocultural, one crop over the whole holding, which only makes sense if that crop is to be sold. Wheat and maize are the major crops, both grain crops traded in bulk.

The economics are commercial too: per hectare yield is low but per capita income is high, which describes a system that makes its return from area and from selling the output rather than from intensive cultivation to feed a family.

Cultivation and commercial animal husbandry are done together, which the chapter elsewhere calls allied activities.

It is practised on the temperate grasslands, the Steppes, Prairies, Downs, Pampas and Velds, all of them thinly peopled regions where the produce must be sent elsewhere to find a market.

Because a coniferous forest is easy to work and a tropical forest is not.

The chapter states the positive reason: in the coniferous forests only one species of trees is found in an area and these trees grow tall, and that is why lumbering is mostly practised in the coniferous regions of the world. A stand of one species can be cut, handled and sold as a single product, and the tall straight trunks suit mechanised felling.

It states the negative reason too: the trees in the tropical forest have hardwood, and these forests are evergreen, hence commercial lumbering cannot be done in them. Table 4.2 adds that dense growth makes them inaccessible and creates transportation problems, that many species in a small area make working them unprofitable, that insects and reptiles cause problems, and that the climate is inhospitable.

Demand settles it. Hard wood is comparatively less in demand than softwood, so even the timber cut in the tropics finds a smaller market than the softwood of the north.

Because of what large-scale hunting did to wildlife.

The chapter states that a large number of animal species have become extinct or are on the verge of extinction because of large-scale hunting. Commercial hunting is therefore banned all over the world, and many laws are being passed to conserve and protect the animals.

The ban is on commercial hunting. The chapter notes that some tribes still practice hunting for their subsistence, and names the Bushmen of the Kalahari, the Pygmies of the equatorial Selvas, the Boras, the Eskimos of the Tundra, and the Sentinels, Jarawahs and Onges among them.

The wider reason is that hunting takes from nature without replacing anything. A species removed faster than it breeds does not recover, so unlike agriculture or lumbering there is no level at which commercial hunting is sustainable.

| Point of difference | Lumbering in equatorial forests | Lumbering in temperate forests |
|---|---|---|
| Nature of the forest | Dense and evergreen, with many species in a small area | Coniferous forests have only one species in an area, and the trees grow tall |
| Type of wood | Hard wood | Soft wood in the coniferous forests |
| Demand for the wood | Hard wood is comparatively less in demand than softwood | Softwood is in greater demand |
| Accessibility | Difficult; dense forests increase inaccessibility and create transportation issues | Easier, and the regions are better served by transport |
| Climate | Inhospitable and humid, and insects and reptiles cause problems | Cold but workable |
| Methods | Traditional methods of lumbering | Mechanised, since one species over a large area suits machinery |
| Scale | Commercial lumbering cannot be done; the presence of many species in one region makes it unprofitable | The lumbering activity of the world is mostly practised here |
| Regions | Amazon river basin, Congo river basin, West coast of Africa, South East Asia, Papua New Guinea | The far north of North America, Europe and Asia |

| Point of difference | Plantation agriculture | Extensive commercial agriculture |
|---|---|---|
| Region | Tropical, in Malaysia, India, Sri Lanka, Brazil, Indonesia, the Caribbean Islands, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam | Temperate grassland: Steppes, Praries, Downs, Pampas, Velds |
| Crops | Tea, coffee, rubber, cocoa, spices, cashewnut | Wheat and maize |
| Labour | Local labour is employed | Machinery is used from sowing to harvesting |
| Yield and return | Per hectare yield is low but total production is high | Per hectare yield is low but per capita income is high |
| Life of the crop | Once planted it gives production for 10 to 15 years | Sown and harvested each season |
| Processing | The crop is well managed for quality and processing | Grain is sold as harvested |
| Allied activity | None named | Cultivation and commercial animal husbandry are done together |

Both are large, capital-intensive and monocultural, which is what makes them easy to confuse. The differences that matter are the climate belt they occupy, whether the crop is a tree or a grain, and whether the work is done by hand or by machine.

| Point of difference | Mining | Fishing |
|---|---|---|
| What is taken | Minerals from the earth's crust, and oil and natural gas from the sea and ocean beds | Fish from the sea and from inland waters |
| Is the resource renewable? | No; man cannot manufacture the minerals found naturally in the earth's crust | Yes, fish breed and replace themselves |
| Relation to latitude | None; the activity depends solely on the presence of minerals and is not related to latitude directly | Strong; it follows the shelves, the banks and the meeting of warm and cold currents |
| What decides where it happens | The distribution of minerals, which is highly uneven in the world | A wide continental shelf with shallow water, and the confluence of warm and cold currents with the growth of plankton |

The chapter divides them into physical and human factors.

The physical factors it names first are two. A wide expanse of the continental shelf with the presence of shallow water, its example being the north-west Pacific below 200 metres of depth near the Okhotsk Sea near China. And the confluence of warm and cold currents with the subsequent growth of abundant plankton, as a result of which fishing grounds or banks develop, its example being the meeting of the warm Kuroshio current with the cold Oyashio current which favours the coastal area near Japan.

The further factors it lists are these.

Traditional skills. Some people are naturally good at fishing, for example the Japanese and the Chinese, and the activity has developed further there.

Dependence on fish as food. A large population, a lack of land and the absence of other protein food make island countries especially dependent on fish as a staple food, for example Japan and the Philippines.

Absence of an alternative occupation, which makes fishing a major occupation.

Use of technology, which has increased fishing activity.

A broken coast line, which provides excellent port facilities.

A cold climate in the temperate regions, which facilitates the preservation of fish; in tropical countries artificial refrigeration facilities have to be developed instead.

Nearby forest, which provides wood for ship building.

The chapter notes that fishing started as a subsistence level activity and is now one of the major primary economic activities, especially in coastal areas.

Intensive subsistence agriculture is cultivation on small holdings worked to their limit, chiefly to feed the family that farms them.

Its land holdings are small, and the maximum yield is taken from a small area of land. Food crops are dominant, and rice is the major crop.

The work is done by manual labour and by the use of animals rather than by machinery, which is possible because the holdings are small and labour is plentiful.

It is practised in China, India, Japan, Korea, Sri Lanka and the East Asian countries, that is in the monsoon lands where rainfall is reliable and the population is dense.

The name states its character. It is intensive because effort and inputs per hectare are high, and subsistence because the produce is grown mainly for consumption rather than for sale. This is the form that lies behind the chapter's observation that the share of population engaged in agriculture is higher in developing countries.

Market gardening is a modern type of agriculture that grows perishable produce for a nearby city.

It is developed in fringe areas, in order to fulfil the demands of urban people, and it is found mainly in highly industrialised and densely populated urban areas.

Maximum production is taken from a limited agricultural area. The use of capital is high, and along with manual labour it uses scientific technology and knowledge. Organic and chemical manures or fertilizers and irrigation are used.

Its distance from the market is part of its definition: it is practised in areas lying at the distance of an overnight journey by trucks, because the produce must reach the city fresh.

The produce is vegetables, fruits, milk, eggs, meat and fish. The chapter's example is fruit, vegetables and flowers brought to Pune from Khedshivapur and Saswad.

Commercial animal husbandry has developed in North America, South America and Australia, which the chapter names directly.

In North and South America it is carried out with the help of advanced technology on a commercial scale.

What these regions share is the temperate grasslands of the continental interiors, and the chapter states that the presence of grasslands in all the continents has led to the distribution of this occupation. Latitudinally it lies between 30 and 60 degrees N and between 30 and 55 degrees S, and it is more developed in the northern hemisphere.

Three things turn grazing into a commercial industry, and the chapter names them: advanced technology, market, and the availability of large estates. The thinly peopled interiors of these continents supply the last of the three.

The regions where it has not developed show the same reasoning from the other side. Dense forests, an inhospitable climate and low-quality fodder in the equatorial region have discouraged it there.

The chapter adds that agriculture and animal husbandry are done together in many areas, which is why the two are considered allied activities.

Mining is unlike the other primary activities in that its raw material cannot be grown or replaced.

The chapter states that man cannot manufacture the minerals that are found naturally in the earth's crust. They exist where geology put them, their distribution is highly uneven in the world, and the activity depends solely on the presence of minerals. That is why mining shows no latitudinal pattern, unlike lumbering, fishing, agriculture and animal husbandry, all of which follow climate.

Presence alone is not enough, however. Even though the minerals may be present, actual mining depends on several factors: the geology of the region, the value of the minerals, climate, capital investment, technology and skilled labour. A low-value deposit in difficult ground may be left untouched.

The activity has widened with technology. Due to mechanisation it has developed on a large scale, and man has even started exploiting mineral oil and natural gas reserves from the sea and ocean beds.

Its consequences reach beyond itself. Many industries related to minerals locate near mining areas, improved transportation facilities are very important for its development, and this in turn increases industries, which leads to the economic development of the country. The chapter also ties minerals to the whole cultural evolution of man, naming the Copper Age, the Bronze Age, the Iron Age and the Atomic Age after them.

The primary economic activities are hunting, gathering, animal husbandry, agriculture, fishing, lumbering and mining. Their characteristics are these.

They take directly from nature. The chapter states that all these activities are dependent on nature, and that natural resources are exploited in them. Nothing is manufactured at this stage; what is produced is a raw material.

They are governed by physical conditions. Climate, relief, soil, water and vegetation decide where each can be carried on, which is why the map shows each activity in its own belt or region rather than spread evenly.

Mining is the exception that proves the rule. It depends solely on the presence of minerals and is not related to latitude directly, because minerals were placed by geology rather than by climate.

They are vulnerable to nature as well as dependent on it. The chapter notes that the effect of natural calamities affects these primary activities.

They are the oldest occupations of man. Hunting was a primitive activity of man to obtain food, and fishing started as a subsistence level activity before becoming a major economic one.

They are being mechanised. To fulfil the needs of a growing population and to provide technical help to manpower, mechanization was started in primary activities.

Their share of employment marks a country's development. The proportion of people engaged is maximum in Africa and then in Asia, while in Europe, the Americas and Australia the percentage of population engaged is very less; generally the developed countries have less population engaged in agriculture while the share is higher in developing countries.

Many of them are allied to one another. Agriculture and animal husbandry are done together in many areas, and the chapter calls them allied activities for that reason.

A simple bar diagram is the suitable choice, because six independent percentages have to be compared with one another.

Draw the six continents along the X-axis, leaving equal gaps between them. Take percentage of population engaged in primary economic activities on the Y-axis, from 0 to 50. Draw one bar for each continent to the same scale, shade them alike, and give the diagram the title 'Continent-wise employment in primary economic activities, 2018' with the source noted as FAO data, 2018.

The heights to plot are Europe 7.91, North America 14.93, South America 14.94, Asia 24.49, Australia 27.79 and Africa 47.28.

Drawing the bars in ascending order of height makes the pattern easier to read, since the figures then run from the most developed continent to the least.

A pie chart would not serve here, because the six figures are separate percentages of six different populations and do not add to 100.
Europe alone, with 7.91 per cent. Every other continent in the table is above 14 per cent.

Africa, with 47.28 per cent, which is nearly half its population and well above the next highest, Australia at 27.79 per cent.

The chapter states the same thing in prose: the proportion of people engaged in agriculture is maximum in Africa and then in Asia.

Yes, by reading the figures in reverse: the smaller the share of population in primary activities, the more developed the continent.

In ascending order of economic development, that is from least to most developed:

Africa (47.28), Australia (27.79), Asia (24.49), South America (14.94), North America (14.93), Europe (7.91).

The chapter supplies the principle. It states that generally the developed countries of the world have less population engaged in agriculture while the share of population engaged in agriculture is higher in developing countries, and that the area under agriculture is extensive in Europe, the Americas and Australia even though the percentage of population engaged in it there is very less.

The ranking has to be read with care in two places. North America and South America differ by only 0.01 percentage point, so this measure cannot really separate them. And Australia sits second from the bottom at 27.79 per cent, which does not match its standing by any other measure of development; the chapter itself groups Australia with Europe and the Americas as a region where the area under agriculture is extensive but the population engaged is small.

That is the wider lesson: a single indicator can rank continents only roughly, and this one misplaces Australia.
